# EDA Template (R, beginner version)

**Contents** (the big sections)

0.  Packages and settings (edit here only)
1.  Read the tables and merge
2.  Check the structure of the data
3.  Split: `raw` and `holdout`
4.  Basic statistics
5.  Distribution plots
6.  Explore with groups
7.  Correlation between variables
8.  Overview of missing values
9.  What does the missingness mean?
10. Save the plots and tables
11. New columns, filled missing values, and the files `raw` and `holdout`

- Appendix: basic operations

- Date and time

- Run the chunks from top to bottom. **Change only the settings chunk (section 0)** to reuse this on other data. In section 1 you also write your own file names and joins, and in 2-3 you choose option A or option B.

- **The order matters: merge the tables (1) -\> look at the structure (2) -\> cut the rows into `raw` and `holdout` (3) -\> explore `raw` only (4-10) -\> on ALL the rows (`full`): fill the missing values, make the new columns, and save `raw` and `holdout` (11).** The holdout is not used for anything until the very end of the analysis template.

- Example data: the bike data (`rentals.csv`, `stations.csv`, `weather.csv`). In the code, names like `temp_c`, `station_type`, `district`, `opened_date` are written directly (they were `age`, `gender`, `region_id`, `signup_date` in the customer example). For other data, replace them with your own column names.

- Plots are plain base-R plots (`hist`, `barplot`, `boxplot`, `plot`).

- Sections 4-9 are the old sections 2-7 of this template. The original "section 0" reference (Series / DataFrame / select / rename ...) is the **Appendix** at the end.

- Comments saying *(optional)* mark things that only make the output look nicer. You can ignore them.

- The next template is `analysis_template.Rmd`. It reads the files written in section 11 (11-4), the last step.

**What to change for a new data set (and where it is)**

| what | where |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| `TARGET`, `TIME` (`NULL` = no time column), `GROUP` (`NULL` = none) | chunk `settings` (section 0) |
| time or random split, size of the holdout | `settings`: `SPLIT`, `HOLDOUT_FRAC` |
| time-series features of the target (lags ...), optional | `settings`: `TS_MODE`; the chunks are in 11-3 |
| how the missing values are filled | 11-1, chunk `fill-all`: `METHOD` and the lines below it |
| new columns (optional) | 11-2, chunk `new-columns` |
| file names, one `read_csv` per table | 1, chunk `read-tables` |
| which tables are joined, on which keys | 1, chunks `check-keys`, `check-unmatched`, `merge` |
| which columns are NUM / CAT / date / id | **you choose ONE**: option A (you write the lists in `settings`) or option B (automatic), both in 2-3 |
| the examples with column names (`temp_c`, `station_type` ...) | the chunks of sections 4-9: replace the names or skip them |

## 0. Packages and settings (edit here only)

```{r settings}
# install.packages("tidyverse")        # run once if tidyverse is not installed
library(tidyverse)

options(width = 150)                   # (optional) wider printing
options(tibble.print_max = 50)         # (optional) print up to 50 rows of a table
options(tibble.print_min = 20)         # (optional) print at least 20 rows of a table
options(tibble.width = Inf)            # (optional) print all columns of a table

# ===== Settings =====
SEED           <- 0
TARGET         <- "rentals"            # the numeric outcome (y)
TIME           <- "date"               # the time column. NULL if the data has no time column
GROUP          <- "station_id"         # a column whose values repeat (the same station / customer / patient ...). NULL if none
SPLIT          <- "time"               # how the holdout is made: "time" (the LAST part in time) or "random"
HOLDOUT_FRAC   <- 0.2                  # the share of the rows (days) kept as the holdout
TS_MODE        <- "bar"               # time-series features of the target (section 11-3): "none" | "row" (previous rows) | "bar" (previous days / hours)

MISSING_TOKENS <- c("?", "unknown", "N/A", "")   # text values that really mean "missing"
MAX_UNIQUE     <- 15                   # at most this many different values -> a category (used by option B and by the bar charts)

# Option A (you decide): write the lists here. Option B (automatic) overwrites ID_COLS, DATE_COLS, NUM and CAT.
ID_COLS        <- c("rental_id", "station_id")          # ID columns (not predictors)
DATE_COLS      <- c("date", "opened_date")              # date columns
CAT_NUM_COLS   <- c("district_code")                    # columns stored as numbers that are really categories
NUM            <- c("temp_c", "feels_like_c", "humidity", "wind_kmh", "rain_mm", "day_off", "promo",
                    "capacity", "dist_center_km", "bikes_available_am", "random_score")   # numeric predictors
CAT            <- c("station_type", "district", "district_code", "has_charging", "weather_alert", "event_nearby", "station_color")   # categorical predictors
# ====================

HAS_TIME <- !is.null(TIME)
if (!HAS_TIME) TS_MODE <- "none"      # no time column: no time-series features
set.seed(SEED)
```

This chunk is a **cheat sheet** (`eval = FALSE`): run the lines you need one at a time in the console. The R names are `dplyr` / `tibble` functions unless noted.

```{r cheat-sheet, eval=FALSE}
# ===== Vector (= a pandas Series: one column) =====
s <- c(25, 40, 31)                                   # from values
s <- c(a = 25, b = 40, c = 31)                       # named vector (names play the role of the index)
s["b"]; s[2]; s[s > 30]                              # by name / by position (R starts at 1!) / by condition

# ===== Data frame / tibble (= a DataFrame: several columns) =====
df <- tibble(age = c(25, 40, 31), gender = c("F", "M", "F"))             # {column = values}
df <- tribble(~age, ~gender,  25, "F",  40, "M")                         # row by row (easy to read)
df <- bind_rows(list(age = 25, gender = "F"), list(age = 40, gender = "M"))   # list of rows
# df <- read_csv("file.csv")                                            # from a file

# Taking ONE column out
df$age; df[["age"]]; pull(df, age)       # -> vector (same as a Series)
df["age"]; select(df, age)               # -> still a tibble (like df[["age"]] vs df[["age"]] in pandas)
# CAUTION: df[, "age"] gives a vector for a data.frame but a tibble for a tibble.

# ===== Selecting columns (after reading) =====
select(df, age, gender)                              # by name
df[c("age", "gender")]                               # base R
select(df, -gender)                                  # everything except gender
select(df, 1, 3)                                     # by position
select(df, where(is.numeric))                        # by type: is.character / is.factor / is.logical / lubridate::is.Date
select(df, contains("age"))                          # name contains "age"; also starts_with() ends_with() matches("regex")
cols <- c("age", "gender"); select(df, all_of(cols)) # from a character vector of names (the way this template does it)
cols <- setdiff(names(df), "customer_id")            # "all columns except ..."

# ===== Renaming columns =====
rename(df, customer_age = age, sex = gender)         # rename(NEW = OLD)  <- opposite order from pandas {old: new}
names(df) <- c("a", "b")                             # replace all names (count and order must match)
rename_with(df, ~ str_replace_all(str_to_lower(str_trim(.x)), " ", "_"))   # rule-based: trim, lower case, spaces -> _
rename_with(df, ~ paste0("c_", .x))                  # add a prefix to every column;  paste0(.x, "_raw") for a suffix
# janitor::clean_names(df) does the "snake_case" rule in one call (needs the janitor package)

# ===== Reordering columns =====
select(df, gender, age)                              # list them in the new order (only the listed ones are kept)
relocate(df, gender)                                 # move gender to the front, keep the rest
relocate(df, gender, .after = age)                   # put gender right after age

# ===== Adding and removing columns =====
df <- mutate(df, age2 = age * 2,                     # compute a new column
                 flag  = 0,                          # same value in every row
                 group = if_else(age >= 30, "old", "young"))   # conditional value (like np.where)
# case_when(age < 20 ~ "teen", age < 60 ~ "adult", TRUE ~ "senior")   # several conditions
df <- select(df, -age2, -flag)                       # remove columns
s  <- df$group; df$group <- NULL                     # take a column out and remove it (like pandas pop)

# ===== Changing column types =====
mutate(df, age = as.numeric(age), gender = as.factor(gender))
mutate(df, d = as.Date(d, format = "%Y-%m-%d"))      # %Y = 4-digit year, %y = 2-digit year, %m, %d, %H:%M:%S
mutate(df, d = lubridate::ymd(d))                    # also ymd_hms(), mdy(), dmy(); bad values become NA with a warning
# as.numeric("abc") gives NA with a warning -> check with is.na() afterwards

# ===== Selecting rows =====
filter(df, age > 30)                                 # by condition (NA conditions are dropped)
df[df$age > 30, ]                                    # base R (CAUTION: NA conditions give NA rows)
filter(df, age > 30) %>% select(age, gender)         # condition + columns
head(df, 3); slice(df, 1:3)                          # first 3 rows / rows by position
slice_sample(df, n = 5)                              # random 5 rows (call set.seed() first for reproducibility)
filter(df, age %in% c(25, 31)); filter(df, between(age, 25, 35))

# ===== Removing rows =====
slice(df, -c(1, 3))                                  # drop rows 1 and 3 by position
filter(df, !(age > 120))                             # drop rows by condition (= keep the others)
# DANGER: df[-which(df$age > 120), ] returns ZERO rows when nothing matches. Prefer filter(df, !(age > 120)).

# ===== Row names / "index" =====
# Tibbles have no index: keep the ID as an ordinary column (merging and grouping are done with columns).
tibble::column_to_rownames(as.data.frame(df), "customer_id")   # column -> row names (data.frame only)
tibble::rownames_to_column(as.data.frame(df), "customer_id")   # row names -> column

# ===== Selecting by string pattern (stringr) =====
x <- c("Mouse", "Laptop", "Keyboard", "Monitor", "Headphones")
str_starts(x, "M")                  # starts with M
str_ends(x, "er")                   # ends with "er"
str_detect(x, "ou")                 # contains "ou" anywhere (the pattern is a regular expression)
str_detect(x, "^(M|L)")             # starts with M or L
```

## 1. Read the tables and merge

The data often comes in several tables. They are merged into ONE table `df` (one row = one unit of analysis) **first**. Here: one row = one station on one day (`rentals`), the station information (`stations`) and the weather of the day (`weather`) are attached.

| join | keeps | use it when |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| `left_join(a, b)` | all rows of `a`; the columns of `b` where the key matches (NA if not) | you want to keep all rows of the main table (the usual case) |
| `inner_join(a, b)` | only the rows whose key is in both | you want only the matched rows |
| `full_join(a, b)` | all rows of both | you want everything |

**A left join must not change the number of rows of the main table.** If it does, a key is duplicated in `b`: check the keys first.

```{r read-tables}
rentals  <- read_csv("rentals.csv")      # the main table: one row = one station on one day
stations <- read_csv("stations.csv")     # one row = one station
weather  <- read_csv("weather.csv")      # one row = one day

# Other formats:  read_csv2("x.csv") for ";"  |  read_tsv("x.tsv") for tab  |  readxl::read_excel("x.xlsx") for Excel
# ONE table only?  df <- read_csv("file.csv")  and go on with section 2 (skip the rest of section 1).

glimpse(rentals); glimpse(stations); glimpse(weather)     # a first look at every table
```

```{r check-keys}
# Key check: the key of the "one" side must be unique (if not, rows multiply after the merge)
anyDuplicated(stations$station_id) == 0      # TRUE = every station_id appears once
anyDuplicated(weather$date) == 0             # TRUE = every date appears once

# If there are duplicates, keep only the first row of each key:
stations <- distinct(stations, station_id, .keep_all = TRUE)
```

```{r check-unmatched}
# Rows of the main table whose key is NOT in the other table (they get NA after a left join)
nrow(anti_join(rentals, stations, by = "station_id"))
nrow(anti_join(rentals, weather,  by = "date"))
```

```{r merge}
df <- rentals %>%
  left_join(stations, by = "station_id") %>%
  left_join(weather,  by = "date")

nrow(rentals); nrow(df)                        # must be the same
stopifnot(nrow(df) == nrow(rentals))
head(df)
```

## 2. Check the structure of the data

The merged table `df` is looked at **before** the split: only its structure (types, which values exist, missing values). The distributions and relationships are explored on `raw` only (sections 4-9).

### 2-1. First look

```{r first-look}
dim(df)              # number of rows and number of columns
names(df)            # column names
sapply(df, class)    # type of each column
sapply(df, n_distinct)   # number of different values in each column
head(df)             # first 6 rows
tail(df, 3)          # last 3 rows
glimpse(df)          # name, type and first values of every column
```

```{r look-values}
# The different values (and how often) of every column that has few of them. Look for "?", "unknown", "N/A", the same word spelled in two ways ...
for (col in names(df)) {
  if (n_distinct(df[[col]]) <= MAX_UNIQUE) print(table(df[[col]], useNA = "ifany", dnn = col))
}
# A text column that is mostly numbers: the values that are NOT numbers (for example a "?")
for (col in names(df)[sapply(df, is.character)]) {
  x <- df[[col]][!is.na(df[[col]])]
  not_num <- unique(x[is.na(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x)))])
  if (length(not_num) > 0 && length(not_num) < length(unique(x)) / 2) cat(col, ": mostly numbers, but these are not numbers:", not_num, "\n")
}
```

### 2-2. Fake missing values

A text that really means "missing" (`?`, `unknown`, `N/A` ...) is written in `MISSING_TOKENS` (settings); here it becomes a real `NA`. The chunk above showed which texts there are.

```{r fix-tokens}
for (col in names(df)) {
  if (is.character(df[[col]])) df[[col]][df[[col]] %in% MISSING_TOKENS] <- NA
}
# One column only:  df$station_type[df$station_type %in% c("?", "unknown")] <- NA
```

### 2-3. Which columns are numeric / categorical / date / id? (choose ONE option)

**Option A: you decide.** You wrote `NUM`, `CAT`, `ID_COLS`, `DATE_COLS` and `CAT_NUM_COLS` in the settings chunk. This chunk only applies them. **Run this chunk OR the chunk of option B, not both.**

```{r kinds-manual}
for (col in DATE_COLS)    df[[col]] <- as.Date(df[[col]], format = "%Y-%m-%d")   # text -> date. Other format: "%d/%m/%Y" = 31/01/2024 | "%y" = 2-digit year
for (col in NUM)          df[[col]] <- as.numeric(df[[col]])                      # a column with a "?" was read as text: make it numbers (the fake ones are NA now)
for (col in CAT_NUM_COLS) df[[col]] <- as.factor(df[[col]])                       # numbers that are really categories -> factor

num_cols   <- c(TARGET, NUM)                                                      # numeric columns used in the EDA below (the outcome included)
cat_cols   <- CAT
small_cats <- cat_cols[sapply(df[cat_cols], n_distinct) <= MAX_UNIQUE]            # categories with few different values (bar charts, group summaries)

num_cols; cat_cols; small_cats; DATE_COLS; ID_COLS
sapply(df, class)
```

**Option B: automatic.** The code guesses the kinds from the data and **overwrites** `ID_COLS`, `DATE_COLS`, `NUM` and `CAT`. Run this chunk only if you do not want to write the lists yourself.

```{r kinds-auto}
# 1. text columns that are really numbers (more than 90% of the values parse as numbers, e.g. a column that had a "?") -> numeric
for (col in names(df)) {
  if (is.character(df[[col]])) {
    as_num <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(df[[col]]))
    has_value <- !is.na(df[[col]])
    if (any(has_value) && mean(!is.na(as_num[has_value])) > 0.9) df[[col]] <- as_num
  }
}

# 2. text columns that look like dates (more than 90% of the values match) -> Date
#    (read_csv already turns "2024-01-31" columns into Date; this catches the rest. Change the format if needed.)
for (col in names(df)) {
  if (is.character(df[[col]])) {
    as_date <- as.Date(df[[col]], format = "%Y-%m-%d")
    has_value <- !is.na(df[[col]])
    if (any(has_value) && mean(!is.na(as_date[has_value])) > 0.9) df[[col]] <- as_date
  }
}

# 3. find the ID columns: the name ends with "id" AND there are many different values
# grepl: Check whether a string contains a pattern; ^ = starts with, $ = ends with,  ignore.case = dont distinguish lower and upper letter.
id_like  <- grepl("id$", names(df), ignore.case = TRUE) & sapply(df, n_distinct) > MAX_UNIQUE
id_cols  <- names(df)[id_like]

# 4. numeric columns with few different values are really categories -> factor (not the outcome)
#    (if a real number column is turned into a category by mistake, lower MAX_UNIQUE)
few_values <- sapply(df, function(x) is.numeric(x) && n_distinct(x) <= MAX_UNIQUE)
for (col in names(df)[few_values & !id_like & names(df) != TARGET]) df[[col]] <- as.factor(df[[col]])

# 5. column kinds
date_cols  <- names(df)[sapply(df, function(x) inherits(x, c("Date", "POSIXct")))]
num_cols   <- setdiff(names(df)[sapply(df, is.numeric)], id_cols)               # numeric
cat_cols   <- setdiff(names(df), c(num_cols, date_cols, id_cols))               # categorical
small_cats <- cat_cols[sapply(df[cat_cols], n_distinct) <= MAX_UNIQUE]          # categories with few values

# the lists the analysis template needs
ID_COLS   <- id_cols
DATE_COLS <- date_cols
NUM       <- setdiff(num_cols, TARGET)
CAT       <- setdiff(small_cats, GROUP)

NUM; CAT; ID_COLS; DATE_COLS
sapply(df, class)
```

### 2-4. Column summary, unique values, duplicates

```{r column-summary}
# One row per column: type / number of different values / number of missing values
data.frame(type      = sapply(df, function(x) class(x)[1]),    # function(x) means "for each column x"
           n_unique  = sapply(df, n_distinct),
           n_missing = colSums(is.na(df)))
```

```{r unique-values}
# Different values (and how often each appears) of the category-like columns:
# categorical columns + numeric columns with at most MAX_UNIQUE different values
few_value_nums <- num_cols[sapply(df[num_cols], n_distinct) <= MAX_UNIQUE]

for (col in c(small_cats, few_value_nums)) {
  print(table(df[[col]], useNA = "ifany", dnn = col))      # dnn = col puts the column name above the table, useNA : count NA if there exists NA.
}
```

```{r duplicates}
sum(duplicated(df))                         # fully duplicated rows
for (col in ID_COLS) {
  print(sum(duplicated(df[[col]])))         # duplicated IDs, one number per ID column
}

df[duplicated(df$rental_id), ]              # look at the duplicated rows
# df <- distinct(df)                        # remove fully duplicated rows
```

### 2-5. (Optional) Date parts

Done on a copy (`temp`), so `df` does not change.

```{r date-parts}
WEEK_ORDER <- c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")

temp <- df
d <- temp$opened_date                                     # the date column
range(d, na.rm = TRUE)                                    # first and last date
sum(is.na(d))                                             # number of missing dates

temp$opened_year    <- as.numeric(format(d, "%Y"))
temp$opened_month   <- as.numeric(format(d, "%m"))
temp$opened_weekday <- WEEK_ORDER[as.numeric(format(d, "%u"))]      # %u: Monday = 1 ... Sunday = 7

#or temp$opened_weekday <- factor(WEEK_ORDER[as.numeric(format(temp$opened_date, "%u"))], levels = WEEK_ORDER)
temp$opened_hour    <- as.numeric(format(d, "%H"))                  # a Date has no time -> always 0
temp$opened_is_weekend <- as.numeric(format(d, "%u")) >= 6          # TRUE for Saturday / Sunday

table(factor(temp$opened_weekday, levels = WEEK_ORDER))   # number of rows per weekday, in weekday order
table(temp$opened_month)                                  # number of rows per month

# The difference between two dates is a number of days: how long the station has been open on the day of the row
temp$station_age_days <- as.numeric(temp$date - temp$opened_date)   # (the same column is made on `full` in section 11-2, for the models)
range(temp$station_age_days, na.rm = TRUE)                          # the shortest and the longest
```

## 3. Split: `raw` and `holdout`

From here on the rows are in **two** groups:

- `raw`: the rows that we explore (sections 4-10), select variables on, cross-validate and fit on.
- `holdout`: kept aside. **Do not use it in sections 4-10.** It stays inside the table `full` (= all the rows, every row has a label `.part`: `"raw"` or `"holdout"`); the last section (11) fills the missing values and makes the new columns on `full`, so that `raw` and `holdout` get exactly the same, and only then cuts them out again and **saves** the two files.

| `SPLIT` | when | how |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| `"time"` | the data has a time column (`TIME`) | `holdout` = the **last** days (the last `HOLDOUT_FRAC` of the days). A day is never cut in two |
| `"random"` | no time column, or the rows do not depend on time | `holdout` = random rows |

```{r split}
if (SPLIT == "time" && HAS_TIME) {
  df   <- df[order(df[[TIME]]), ]                       # sort by time
  day  <- as.Date(df[[TIME]])
  days <- sort(unique(day))                             # the different days
  hold_start <- days[floor(length(days) * (1 - HOLDOUT_FRAC)) + 1]     # the first day of the holdout
  df$.part <- ifelse(day >= hold_start, "holdout", "raw")
} else {
  rows <- sample(nrow(df), floor(nrow(df) * (1 - HOLDOUT_FRAC)))       # random rows (the same every time: set.seed)
  df$.part <- "holdout"
  df$.part[rows] <- "raw"
}
full    <- df                                                          # ALL the rows, with the label of every row
raw     <- full[full$.part == "raw",     names(full) != ".part"]
holdout <- full[full$.part == "holdout", names(full) != ".part"]

cat("raw:", nrow(raw), "rows | holdout:", nrow(holdout), "rows\n")
if (HAS_TIME) cat("raw:", format(min(raw[[TIME]])), "to", format(max(raw[[TIME]])), "| holdout:", format(min(holdout[[TIME]])), "to", format(max(holdout[[TIME]])), "\n")

df <- raw         # from now on df = raw: the EDA below uses df
```

## 4. Basic statistics

```{r stats-numeric}
# Numeric columns: one row per column
round(data.frame(count  = colSums(!is.na(df[num_cols])),
                 mean   = sapply(df[num_cols], mean,   na.rm = TRUE),     # na.rm = TRUE ignores missing values
                 sd     = sapply(df[num_cols], sd,     na.rm = TRUE),
                 min    = sapply(df[num_cols], min,    na.rm = TRUE),
                 median = sapply(df[num_cols], median, na.rm = TRUE),
                 max    = sapply(df[num_cols], max,    na.rm = TRUE)), 2)

# With percentiles (5%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 95%)
round(t(sapply(df[num_cols], quantile, probs = c(.05, .25, .5, .75, .95), na.rm = TRUE)), 2)

summary(df[num_cols])        # quick version (quartiles + number of NA)
```

```{r stats-by-station_type}
# The same statistics by station_type (rows with missing station_type are not shown)


df %>%
  group_by(station_type) %>%
  summarise(n      = n(),                          # number of rows in the group (NA ages included)
            n_age  = sum(!is.na(temp_c)),             # number of rows where temp_c is present
            mean   = mean(temp_c, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd     = sd(temp_c, na.rm = TRUE),
            median = median(temp_c, na.rm = TRUE),
            min    = min(temp_c, na.rm = TRUE),
            max    = max(temp_c, na.rm = TRUE))

aggregate(df[num_cols], by = list(station_type = df$station_type), FUN = mean,   na.rm = TRUE)
aggregate(df[num_cols], by = list(station_type = df$station_type), FUN = sd,     na.rm = TRUE)
aggregate(df[num_cols], by = list(station_type = df$station_type), FUN = median, na.rm = TRUE)
aggregate(df[num_cols], by = list(station_type = df$station_type), FUN = min,    na.rm = TRUE)
aggregate(df[num_cols], by = list(station_type = df$station_type), FUN = max,    na.rm = TRUE)

# By two columns
aggregate(df[num_cols], by = list(station_type = df$station_type, district = df$district), FUN = mean, na.rm = TRUE)

# Counts
table(df$station_type, useNA = "ifany")         # number of rows per station_type (NA is counted too)
count(df, station_type)                         # same, as a table
count(df, station_type, district)              # number of rows per station_type and region
```

```{r stats-categorical}
# Categorical columns: count and percent (NA is shown as its own row)
for (col in small_cats) {
  counts <- table(df[[col]], useNA = "ifany", dnn = col)
  print(cbind(count = counts, pct = round(100 * counts / nrow(df), 1)))
}
```

```{r stats-dates}
# Date columns: first and last date
for (col in DATE_COLS) {
  print(range(df[[col]], na.rm = TRUE))
}
```

## 5. Distribution plots

`las = 2` turns the labels on the axis so that they do not overlap. If category names are long (like the months below), also enlarge the bottom margin with `par(mar = c(7, 4, 4, 2))` and move the x title down with `title(xlab = "...", line = 5.5)`.

```{r plots-hist}
# Histogram of the target (it is also the first plot of the loop below, because num_cols starts with the target)
hist(df[[TARGET]], breaks = 25, main = paste("Histogram of the target:", TARGET), xlab = TARGET, ylab = "count")
# hist(log(df[[TARGET]] + 1), breaks = 25, main = paste("Histogram of log(", TARGET, "+ 1 )"), xlab = paste("log(", TARGET, "+ 1 )"), ylab = "count")   # (optional) if the target is skewed

# Histogram of every numeric column (one plot per column)
for (col in num_cols) {
  hist(df[[col]], breaks = 25, main = paste("Histogram of", col), xlab = col, ylab = "count")
}

for (col in num_cols) {
  for (g in na.omit(unique(df$station_type))) {
    hist(df[[col]][df$station_type == g],
         breaks = 25,
         main = paste("Histogram of", col, "-", g),
         xlab = col,
         ylab = "count")
  }
}
```

```{r plots-bar}
# Bar chart of every category column with few values
for (col in small_cats) {
  barplot(table(df[[col]], useNA = "ifany"), main = paste("Count of", col), xlab = col, ylab = "count", las = 2)
}

df$station_type <- factor(df$station_type, levels = names(sort(table(df$station_type), decreasing = TRUE)))   # the most frequent first (or: levels = c("a", "b"))
barplot(table(df$station_type, useNA = "ifany"),
        main = "Count of station_type", xlab = "station_type", ylab = "count")
```

```{r plots-other}
# Boxplot: a number by category
boxplot(temp_c ~ station_type, data = df, main = "temp_c by station_type", xlab = "station_type", ylab = "temp_c")

# A number over time
plot(df$opened_date, df$temp_c, main = "temp_c over time", xlab = "opened_date", ylab = "temp_c")

# Number of rows per month
# Long labels need room: make the bottom margin bigger (mar) and put the x title lower (line = 5.5), so nothing overlaps.
par(mar = c(7, 4, 4, 2))
barplot(table(format(df$opened_date, "%Y-%m")), main = "rows per month", xlab = "", ylab = "count", las = 2, cex.names = 0.7)
title(xlab = "month", line = 5.5)
par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2))                      # back to the default margins
```

### 5-1. The target over time (month)

x = the month, y = the target. One point per month: the **mean** of the target over all the rows of that month. To use the **day** instead of the month, use the `# day` line and comment out the `# month` line. ggplot chooses the x labels itself, and `check.overlap` leaves out any label that would overlap.

```{r plot-target-time}
if (HAS_TIME) {
  tmp <- df                                                                   # a copy: df does not change
  tmp$period <- lubridate::floor_date(as.Date(tmp[[TIME]]), "month")          # month: the first day of the month of every row
  # tmp$period <- as.Date(tmp[[TIME]])                                        # day: use this line INSTEAD of the line above
  tmp_mean <- aggregate(list(y = tmp[[TARGET]]), by = list(period = tmp$period), FUN = mean, na.rm = TRUE)   # the mean of the target in every period
  ggplot(tmp_mean, aes(x = period, y = y)) +
    geom_line() + geom_point() +
    scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%Y-%m", guide = guide_axis(check.overlap = TRUE)) +
    labs(x = "period", y = paste("mean of", TARGET), title = paste("Mean of", TARGET, "by period"))
}
```

### 5-2. (Optional) The target over time, one color per category

Like 5-1 (x = the month, y = the mean of the target), but with **one line of its own color for every value of a category column**, all in ONE plot. Write the category column in `GROUP_VAR` (the only line to edit). The chunk names a specific column, so it is `eval = FALSE`: it is not run when you knit. For the day instead of the month, use the `# day` line and comment out the `# month` line. With many values (more than 8-10) the lines are hard to read: pick a column with few values.

```{r plot-target-time-color, eval=FALSE}
GROUP_VAR <- "station_type"      # <-- CHANGE HERE: the categorical column to color by (the only line you need to edit)

if (HAS_TIME) {
  tmp <- df                                                                   # a copy: df does not change
  tmp$period <- lubridate::floor_date(as.Date(tmp[[TIME]]), "month")          # month: the first day of the month of every row
  # tmp$period <- as.Date(tmp[[TIME]])                                        # day: use this line INSTEAD of the line above
  tmp$grp <- as.character(tmp[[GROUP_VAR]])                                   # the group of every row (a 0/1 number works too)
  tmp$grp[is.na(tmp$grp)] <- "NA"                                             # missing group = its own color (delete this line to drop it)
  tmp_mean <- aggregate(list(y = tmp[[TARGET]]), by = list(period = tmp$period, grp = tmp$grp), FUN = mean, na.rm = TRUE)   # the mean of the target per period and per group
  ggplot(tmp_mean, aes(x = period, y = y, color = grp)) +                     # color = one line per group
    geom_line() + geom_point() +
    scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%Y-%m", guide = guide_axis(check.overlap = TRUE)) +
    labs(x = "period", y = paste("mean of", TARGET), color = GROUP_VAR, title = paste("Mean of", TARGET, "by period and", GROUP_VAR))
}
```

### 5-3. The target against every numeric column

x = a numeric column, y = the target: one scatter plot per numeric column (the target itself is skipped). The red line is a smooth trend (`lowess`). (`pairs()` in section 7 has the same pictures, but too small to read.)

```{r plot-target-num}
for (col in setdiff(num_cols, TARGET)) {
  ok <- complete.cases(df[[col]], df[[TARGET]])                    # the rows where both values are present
  plot(df[[col]][ok], df[[TARGET]][ok], pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.3),
       main = paste(TARGET, "vs", col), xlab = col, ylab = TARGET)
  lines(lowess(df[[col]][ok], df[[TARGET]][ok]), col = "red")      # (optional) the trend
}
```

### 5-4. The target against every category column

x = a category column, y = the target: one boxplot per category column (only the columns with few different values, `small_cats`). The labels are turned (`las = 2`) and the bottom margin is bigger, so they do not overlap.

```{r plot-target-cat}
for (col in setdiff(small_cats, TARGET)) {
  par(mar = c(8, 4, 4, 2))                                                    # a bigger bottom margin for the category names
  boxplot(df[[TARGET]] ~ df[[col]], main = paste(TARGET, "by", col), xlab = "", ylab = TARGET, las = 2, cex.axis = 0.8)
  title(xlab = col, line = 6.5)                                               # the x title lower, so nothing overlaps
  par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2))                                                    # back to the default margins
}
```

### 5-5. (Optional) The target with two or three other variables

Plots of **3 or more variables** (the target + 2 or 3 others) with `ggplot2`: `color`, `fill`, `facet_wrap`. Every chunk below names **specific columns** (`temp_c`, `station_type` ... of the bike data), so they are `eval = FALSE`: **they are not run when you knit**. Copy the chunk, write your own column names, and run it by hand. The target is always `.data[[TARGET]]` (it comes from the settings: nothing to change).

| chunk | x | y | color / fill | facet | the kinds of variables |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | number | target | category | none | number x number (the target) x category |
| B | number | target | category | category | number x number (the target) x category x category |
| C | category | target | category | none | category x category x number (the target) |
| D | number | number | the target | category | number x number x number (the target) x category |

Other ways to add a variable: `shape =`, `size =`, `facet_grid(row ~ column)`. A 0/1 number that is really a category: write `factor(promo)` (otherwise ggplot uses a color gradient).

```{r plot-3var-a, eval=FALSE}
# (optional) A: a number (x) and the target (y), colored by a category: is the slope different in every category?
ggplot(df, aes(x = temp_c, y = .data[[TARGET]], color = station_type)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +                                        # one smooth curve per category (method = "lm" for a straight line)
  labs(x = "temp_c", y = TARGET, color = "station_type", title = paste(TARGET, "vs temp_c, by station_type"))
```

```{r plot-3var-b, eval=FALSE}
# (optional) B: the same as A, cut in panels by a second category (facet_wrap)
ggplot(df, aes(x = temp_c, y = .data[[TARGET]], color = station_type)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ weather_alert) +                                    # one panel per weather_alert (NA gets its own panel)
  labs(x = "temp_c", y = TARGET, color = "station_type", title = paste(TARGET, "vs temp_c, by station_type and weather_alert"))
```

```{r plot-3var-c, eval=FALSE}
# (optional) C: two categories and the target: boxplots side by side (x = one category, fill = the other one)
ggplot(df, aes(x = station_type, y = .data[[TARGET]], fill = has_charging)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +       # tilted labels: they do not overlap
  labs(x = "station_type", y = TARGET, fill = "has_charging", title = paste(TARGET, "by station_type and has_charging"))
```

```{r plot-3var-d, eval=FALSE}
# (optional) D: two numbers (x and y) and the target as the COLOR, cut in panels by a category
ggplot(df, aes(x = temp_c, y = humidity, color = .data[[TARGET]])) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1) +
  scale_color_viridis_c() +                                        # the color scale of the target
  facet_wrap(~ station_type) +
  labs(x = "temp_c", y = "humidity", color = TARGET, title = paste(TARGET, "by temp_c and humidity, by station_type"))
```

## 7. Correlation between variables

Needs at least 2 numeric columns.

```{r corr}
if (length(num_cols) >= 2) {
  corr <- cor(df[num_cols], use = "pairwise.complete.obs")     # use all rows that are available for each pair
  print(round(corr, 2))

  pairs(df[num_cols], main = "Scatter plots of every pair")    # scatter plots of every pair
  heatmap(corr, symm = TRUE, Rowv = NA, Colv = NA, margins = c(8, 8), main = "Correlation")   # (optional) colored table of the correlations
  pal <- colorRampPalette(c("blue", "white", "red"))(101)      # the colors of the next heatmap: blue = -1, white = 0, red = +1
  heatmap(corr, symm = TRUE, Rowv = NA, Colv = NA, margins = c(10, 10), col = pal,
          breaks = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 102), main = "Correlation (red = +, blue = -)")
  legend("topleft", legend = c("+1", "0", "-1"), fill = c("red", "white", "blue"),
         title = "corr", bty = "n", cex = 0.9)   # (optional) colored table of the correlations
}
```

```{r corr-pairs}
# The most correlated pairs (absolute value)
if (length(num_cols) >= 2) {
  corr_abs <- abs(cor(df[num_cols], use = "pairwise.complete.obs"))
  corr_abs[lower.tri(corr_abs, diag = TRUE)] <- NA             # keep every pair only once
  pair_table <- as.data.frame(as.table(corr_abs))              # long table: Var1, Var2, Freq (= correlation)
  pair_table <- pair_table[!is.na(pair_table$Freq), ]          # remove the NA rows
  head(pair_table[order(-pair_table$Freq), ], 10)              # sort from the largest, show 10
}
```

## 8. Overview of missing values

Everything below runs on `df`. Pandas names are in the comments. `head(...)` is used where the result has one value per row (otherwise it would print hundreds of lines).

```{r missing-by-column}
# ===== By column =====
head(is.na(df))                                  # TRUE/FALSE per cell, TRUE = missing   (df.isna())
colSums(is.na(df))                               # number of missing per column          (isna().sum())
colMeans(is.na(df))                              # share of missing per column, 0 to 1   (isna().mean())
colSums(!is.na(df))                              # number of non-missing per column      (notna().sum())
colSums(is.na(df)) > 0                           # does the column have any missing?     (isna().any())
colSums(is.na(df)) == nrow(df)                   # is the whole column missing?          (isna().all())
sum(is.na(df))                                   # total number of missing cells         (isna().sum().sum())
sort(colSums(is.na(df)), decreasing = TRUE)      # columns with the most missing first
```

```{r missing-by-row}
# ===== By row =====
head(rowSums(is.na(df)))                         # number of missing per row             (isna().sum(axis=1))
head(rowMeans(is.na(df)))                        # share of missing per row
head(rowSums(is.na(df)) > 0)                     # row has at least one missing?         (isna().any(axis=1))
head(rowSums(is.na(df)) == ncol(df))             # whole row is missing?                 (isna().all(axis=1))
head(complete.cases(df))                         # row has NO missing?                   (notna().all(axis=1))
table(rowSums(is.na(df)))                        # how many rows have 0, 1, 2, ... missing values

# ===== Counts in one line =====
sum(rowSums(is.na(df)) > 0)                      # number of rows with missing values
sum(complete.cases(df))                          # number of rows without missing values
nrow(drop_na(df))                                # same number, using drop_na  : remove rows with missing value
sum(is.na(df$temp_c))                               # number of missing in the temp_c column
mean(is.na(df$temp_c))                              # share of missing in the temp_c column
```

```{r missing-names}
# ===== Column names =====
names(df)[colSums(is.na(df)) > 0]                # columns that have missing values
names(df)[colSums(is.na(df)) == 0]               # columns without missing values
names(df)[colMeans(is.na(df)) > 0.3]             # columns with more than 30% missing

# ===== Look at rows =====
filter(df, is.na(temp_c))                           # rows where temp_c is missing
filter(df, !is.na(temp_c))                          # rows where temp_c is present
df[rowSums(is.na(df)) > 0, ]                     # rows with at least one missing value
df[complete.cases(df), ]                         # rows without any missing value
df[rowSums(is.na(df)) == ncol(df), ]             # rows where everything is missing
df[rowSums(is.na(df)) >= 3, ]                    # rows with 3 or more missing values
filter(df, is.na(temp_c) | is.na(station_type))           # temp_c OR station_type is missing
filter(df, !is.na(temp_c) & !is.na(station_type))         # temp_c AND station_type are both present
```

```{r missing-fix}
# ===== Drop / fill (done on copies, so df does not change) =====
temp <- drop_na(df)                              # drop rows with any missing value
temp <- drop_na(df, temp_c)                         # drop rows where temp_c is missing
# drop_na(df, temp_c, income, station_type)
temp <- df[rowSums(is.na(df)) < ncol(df), ]      # drop rows that are completely missing
temp <- df[rowSums(!is.na(df)) >= 4, ]           # keep rows with at least 4 non-missing values
temp <- df[colSums(is.na(df)) == 0]              # drop the columns that have missing values

temp <- df
temp$temp_c[is.na(temp$temp_c)] <- median(df$temp_c, na.rm = TRUE)       # fill temp_c with the median
temp$station_type <- as.character(temp$station_type)                  # a factor cannot get a new word: make it text first
temp$station_type[is.na(temp$station_type)] <- "Unknown"        # fill station_type with a word
temp <- replace_na(mutate(df, station_type = as.character(station_type)), list(temp_c = 0, station_type = "Unknown"))   # fill several columns at once
```

```{r missing-summary}
# ===== Count and percent per column =====
s <- colSums(is.na(df))                          # number of missing per column
s                                                # all columns
s[s > 0]                                         # only columns that have missing values
sort(s[s > 0], decreasing = TRUE)                # ... most missing first
sum(s > 0)                                       # number of columns with missing values
ncol(df)                                         # total number of columns
colMeans(is.na(df)) * 100                        # percent missing per column

# ===== Rows: how many rows have missing values? =====
row_miss <- rowSums(is.na(df))                   # number of missing per row
sum(row_miss > 0)                                # rows with at least one missing
mean(row_miss > 0) * 100                         # ... as a percent
sum(row_miss == 0)                               # rows without any missing
table(row_miss)                                  # rows with 0, 1, 2, ... missing values
```

```{r missing-pattern}
# ===== Missing patterns: which columns are missing together? =====
cols_na <- names(df)[colSums(is.na(df)) > 0]     # columns that have missing values

# Pattern table: TRUE = missing. Each row is one pattern, Freq = number of rows with that pattern.
# (With many columns this table gets very large. Use only a few columns then.)
pattern <- as.data.frame(table(as.data.frame(is.na(df[cols_na]))))
pattern[pattern$Freq > 0, ]

round(cor(is.na(df[cols_na])), 2)                # near 1 = the columns are missing together
table(age_missing = is.na(df$temp_c), gender_missing = is.na(df$station_type))   # two columns only

```

```{r missing-cat-combo}
# ===== Which CATEGORICAL columns are missing together, and does the TARGET differ between the combinations? =====
N_COMBO  <- 3                                                           # <-- CHANGE HERE (optional): how many categorical columns to combine (2 or 3)
miss_n   <- sort(colSums(is.na(df[cat_cols])), decreasing = TRUE)       # the number of missing values of every categorical column, the highest first
miss_n   <- miss_n[miss_n > 0]
miss_n                                                                  # (look at it: the columns with the most missing values come first)
MISS_CAT <- names(head(miss_n, N_COMBO))                                # the N_COMBO categorical columns with the most missing values
# MISS_CAT <- c("station_type", "weather_alert")                        # (optional) or write the columns you want yourself

if (length(MISS_CAT) >= 1) {
  ind_cols <- paste0(MISS_CAT, "_missing")                              # TRUE = missing, FALSE = present
  tab <- df[TARGET]
  for (j in seq_along(MISS_CAT)) tab[[ind_cols[j]]] <- is.na(df[[MISS_CAT[j]]])
  combo <- tab %>%
    group_by(across(all_of(ind_cols))) %>%                              # every combination of missing / present
    summarise(n           = n(),                                        # number of rows
              pct         = round(100 * n() / nrow(df), 1),             # share of the rows (%)
              target_mean = if (is.numeric(.data[[TARGET]])) round(mean(.data[[TARGET]], na.rm = TRUE), 2) else NA_real_,   # mean of the TARGET in this combination
              .groups = "drop") %>%
    arrange(desc(n))                                                    # the most frequent combination first
  none_missing <- combo$target_mean[rowSums(as.matrix(combo[ind_cols])) == 0]       # the TARGET mean when none of these columns is missing
  combo$diff_vs_none_missing <- if (length(none_missing) == 1) round(combo$target_mean - none_missing, 2) else NA_real_   # the difference from that
  print(as.data.frame(combo))
} else {
  cat("no categorical column has missing values\n")
}
```

```{r missing-picture}
# Picture of the missing cells: red = missing, white = present. One column per variable, one line per row.
image(x = 1:length(cols_na), y = 1:nrow(df), z = t(is.na(df[cols_na])) * 1,
      col = c("white", "red"), axes = FALSE, xlab = "column", ylab = "row", main = "Missing cells (red)")
axis(1, at = 1:length(cols_na), labels = cols_na)
```

## 9. What does the missingness mean?

Compare the rows where a column is missing with the rows where it is not.

```{r missing-meaning}
df$days_since_signup <- as.numeric(max(df$opened_date) - df$opened_date)
num_cols <- c(num_cols, "days_since_signup")         # add it to the list of numeric columns
num_cols
col <- "temp_c"                          # the column to investigate (change it to the column you care about)
m <- is.na(df[[col]])                 # TRUE if missing, FALSE if present (one value per row)
others <- setdiff(num_cols, col)      # the other numeric columns used for the comparison

# 1. Numeric columns: mean in the missing group and in the present group
if (length(others) > 0) {
  mean_missing <- sapply(df[m, others],  mean, na.rm = TRUE)
  mean_present <- sapply(df[!m, others], mean, na.rm = TRUE)
  print(data.frame(mean_missing, mean_present))
  
  mean_present2 <- mean_present[names(mean_missing)]     # following the same order as mean_missing
  data.frame(mean_missing, mean_present = mean_present2)

  # (mean of missing group - mean of present group) / overall sd
  # The larger the absolute value, the bigger the difference (below 0.2: tiny, above 0.8: large)   #This standard is proposed by Cohen 
  print(round((mean_missing - mean_present) / sapply(df[others], sd, na.rm = TRUE), 3)) 
}
```

```{r missing-meaning-cat}
# 2. Categorical columns: missing rate by group (TRUE counts as 1, so the mean is the share)
tapply(m, df$district, mean)                            # share of missing in each region
tapply(m, df$station_type, mean)                               # share of missing for each station_type

table(df$district, m)                                   # counts (columns: FALSE = present, TRUE = missing)
round(prop.table(table(df$district, m), margin = 1), 3) # share inside each region (rows sum to 1)
```

```{r missing-meaning-levels}
# 2b. The levels of the other categorical columns inside the two groups: the rows where `col` is missing (TRUE) and the rows where it is present (FALSE)
#     (uses `col` and `m` of the chunk missing-meaning above. Every group adds up to 100%: a level that is more common in one group shows up in the diff column)
if (sum(m) > 0 && sum(!m) > 0) {
  for (cc in setdiff(small_cats, col)) {
    tab  <- table(df[[cc]], m, useNA = "ifany")                          # counts: rows = the levels, columns = FALSE (present) / TRUE (missing)
    pct  <- round(100 * prop.table(tab, margin = 2), 1)                  # % inside each group (every column adds up to 100)
    lv   <- rownames(pct);  lv[is.na(lv)] <- "NA"                        # a missing level is shown as "NA"
    rownames(pct) <- lv
    show <- data.frame(level = lv, present = as.numeric(pct[, "FALSE"]), missing = as.numeric(pct[, "TRUE"]))
    show$diff <- show$missing - show$present                             # in % points: + = more common among the missing rows
    cat("\n", cc, ": share of every level inside the two groups (%)\n")
    print(show, row.names = FALSE)

    par(mar = c(8, 4, 4, 2))                                             # a bigger bottom margin for the level names
    barplot(t(pct), beside = TRUE, las = 2, cex.names = 0.8, ylim = c(0, max(pct) * 1.25), legend.text = c("present", "missing"),
            main = paste(cc, ": share inside each group,", col, "present vs missing"), ylab = "% of the group")
    par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2))                                             # back to the default margins
  }
} else {
  cat(col, "has no missing values (or only missing values): nothing to compare\n")
}
```

```{r missing-meaning-time}
# 3. Change over time: share of missing (%) in each signup month
month <- format(df$opened_date, "%Y-%m")
missing_by_month <- tapply(m, month, mean) * 100
round(missing_by_month, 1)
par(mar = c(7, 4, 4, 2))                      # bigger bottom margin for the long month labels
barplot(missing_by_month, las = 2, cex.names = 0.7, xlab = "", ylab = "% missing", main = paste("missing", col, "by month"))
title(xlab = "month", line = 5.5)
par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2))                      # back to the default margins
```

```{r missing-over-time}
# 3b. Missing over time: x = the month of the TIME column. For the day instead of the month: use the `# day` line and comment out the `# month` line.
if (HAS_TIME) {
  period <- lubridate::floor_date(as.Date(df[[TIME]]), "month")           # month: the first day of the month of every row
  # period <- as.Date(df[[TIME]])                                         # day: use this line INSTEAD of the line above

  # (1) the share of the rows where a column is missing, in every month: one line per column
  MISS_COLS <- names(which(colSums(is.na(df[c(NUM, CAT)])) > 0))         # <-- CHANGE HERE (optional): the columns to draw, for example c("temp_c", "station_type")
  if (length(MISS_COLS) > 0) {
    share <- NULL
    for (cn in MISS_COLS) {
      s     <- tapply(is.na(df[[cn]]), period, mean)                      # the share of missing values in every month (0 to 1)
      share <- rbind(share, data.frame(period = as.Date(names(s)), share = as.numeric(s), column = cn))
    }
    print(ggplot(share, aes(x = period, y = share, color = column)) +
      geom_line() + geom_point() +
      scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%Y-%m", guide = guide_axis(check.overlap = TRUE)) +
      labs(x = "period", y = "share of the rows that are missing", title = "Missing over time, one line per column"))
  }

  # (2) the mean number of missing columns per row, in every month
  n_miss <- rowSums(is.na(df[c(NUM, CAT)]))                               # the number of missing columns of every row (the predictors)
  avg    <- tapply(n_miss, period, mean)                                  # the mean of it in every month
  avg_df <- data.frame(period = as.Date(names(avg)), mean_missing = as.numeric(avg))
  print(ggplot(avg_df, aes(x = period, y = mean_missing)) +
    geom_line() + geom_point() +
    scale_x_date(date_breaks = "1 month", date_labels = "%Y-%m", guide = guide_axis(check.overlap = TRUE)) +
    labs(x = "period", y = "mean number of missing columns per row", title = "Missing columns per row over time"))
} else {
  cat("there is no time column\n")
}
```

```{r missing-meaning-other}
# 4. Relation with the missingness of the other columns
cor(is.na(df[cols_na]))
round(cor(is.na(df[cols_na]))[col, ], 3)                 # near 1 = missing together with that column
table(this_col = m, other_col = is.na(df$station_type))        # combinations of missing / present
```

The plots above only exist on the screen (or in the knitted html). This section writes the main plots as **png files** and the main tables as **csv files** into the folder `OUT_DIR`. Everything is made from `df` (= `raw`).
